aeo.what_is: Eating disorder with severe food restriction, intense fear of weight gain, and distorted body image leading to dangerously low weight.

content.description: Anorexia Nervosa (AN) is an eating disorder characterized by restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight, intense fear of gaining weight or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, and disturbance in the way one's body weight or shape is experienced, with undue influence of body shape/weight on self-evaluation or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of low body weight.
content.temporal_criteria: Restricting type requires no recurrent binge eating or purging in the last 3 months. Binge-eating/purging type requires recurrent episodes within the last 3 months. Weight must be significantly low considering age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health. No specific minimum duration is required, but patterns must be persistent rather than transient.
content.misdiagnosis_explained: Anorexia nervosa can be missed when someone appears 'normal weight' after significant suppression from a higher baseline, when restriction is framed as athletic discipline, or when medical complaints like amenorrhea are treated without exploring eating behaviors. It can be overdiagnosed when weight loss from medical illness occurs without fear of weight gain or body image disturbance, when ARFID involves restriction without weight/shape concerns, or when culturally/religiously motivated fasting is misinterpreted. The key distinction is the core cognitive feature: overvaluation of weight and shape driving restriction, not just the behavior of eating less.
content.diagnostic_criteria: A. Restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight in the context of age, sex, developmental trajectory, and physical health. B. Intense fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, or persistent behavior that interferes with weight gain, even though underweight. C. Disturbance in the way one’s body weight or shape is experienced, undue influence of body shape/weight on self-evaluation, or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of current low body weight. Specify type (restricting vs. binge-eating/purging) and severity by BMI (adults) or BMI percentile (youth).
content.prevalence: Point prevalence ~0.3–1% in females and lower in males; onset commonly in early to mid-adolescence, but can occur across the lifespan.
content.age_of_onset: Typically 12–18 years; risk peaks around puberty/adolescence.
content.prognosis: Course is variable. Early detection and family-based treatment improve outcomes. Risks include medical instability, osteoporosis, infertility, and increased mortality. Long-term recovery is possible with multidisciplinary care; relapse risk is highest within the first year post-weight restoration.

circuitry: Altered reward and interoceptive processing involving striatum, insula, and anterior cingulate cortex.
Heightened cognitive control networks (dorsolateral/medial prefrontal cortex) associated with rigidity and harm avoidance.
neurochemistry: Serotonergic and dopaminergic signaling differences linked to anxiety, satiety, and reward learning.
Starvation-related hormonal changes (leptin, ghrelin, cortisol) reinforce restrictive behaviors and alter appetite signals.
physiology: Malnutrition affects cardiac function (bradycardia, QTc changes), bone metabolism (low bone density), hematologic status, GI motility, endocrine axes (amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea, low LH/FSH).
neurobiology.genetic_environmental: Substantial heritability with polygenic risk; perfectionism, anxiety traits, and cultural/peer pressures interact with biological vulnerability.

history_psychosocial: Onset and course of restriction, exercise, binge/purge behaviors; weight history; body image concerns and rules/rituals around food.
Stressors, trauma history, perfectionism/rigidity, mood/anxiety symptoms, self-harm/suicidality.
Family dynamics, caregiver involvement, and school/work impact.
medical_assessment: Vitals (orthostatic HR/BP), weight/BMI or pediatric growth curves, temperature; signs of dehydration.
Labs: CBC, CMP, magnesium, phosphorus, calcium; TSH; urinalysis; consider ECG for bradycardia/QTc.
Bone health (DXA) in prolonged illness/amenorrhea; menstrual and endocrine review.
standardized_measures: Eating Disorder Examination-Questionnaire (EDE-Q) or EDE interview.
SCOFF, BDI/PHQ-9 (depression), GAD-7 (anxiety), CIA (Clinical Impairment Assessment).
risk_stratification: Hospitalization/urgent care thresholds: unstable vitals (e.g., HR <50 daytime adolescents/<40 adults; symptomatic orthostasis), arrhythmia/QTc prolongation, electrolyte abnormalities (hypophosphatemia, hypokalemia), syncope, acute food refusal, rapid weight loss, BMI <severe range, suicidality, severe dehydration.
differential_diagnosis: Avoidant/Restrictive Food Intake Disorder (ARFID) without weight/shape overvaluation.
Bulimia Nervosa (normal/overweight range with recurrent binge/purge and overvaluation).
Major Depressive Disorder with appetite loss (not weight/shape-driven), hyperthyroidism, inflammatory bowel disease, diabetes with insulin omission, malignancy.
Body Dysmorphic Disorder (appearance preoccupation focused on non-weight concerns).
evaluation.team_and_process: Multidisciplinary care: medical provider, therapist (CBT-E/FBT), dietitian, psychiatry as needed; coordinate with school/athletics; involve caregivers in youth.

behavioral: Food restriction, calorie counting, rigid rules/rituals around eating, avoidance of high-fat foods.
Excessive exercise or movement, body checking, use of baggy clothing.
Binge eating and/or purging (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics) in binge/purge subtype.
cognitive: Intense fear of weight gain; overvaluation of weight/shape; distorted body image.
Perfectionism, black-and-white thinking, guilt after eating.
physical: Underweight or significant weight loss; fatigue, dizziness, cold intolerance.
Amenorrhea/irregular menses, hair loss, lanugo, constipation, abdominal pain.

severity_levels.mild: Adults: BMI ≥17; adolescents: mild deviation from expected growth trajectory; medically stable.
severity_levels.moderate: Adults: BMI 16–16.99 or notable growth faltering; mild medical instability.
severity_levels.severe: Adults: BMI 15–15.99 with medical concerns; marked functional impairment.
severity_levels.extreme: Adults: BMI <15 or significant medical instability regardless of BMI.

biological: Female sex (though any gender can be affected)
Family history of eating disorders or anxiety/mood disorders
environmental: Diet culture, bullying/teasing about weight, social media pressures

impact_on_life.school_work: Cognitive fog, decreased concentration, absences for medical care, withdrawal from activities.
impact_on_life.social: Avoidance of meals/social events; isolation; conflict around eating.
impact_on_life.medical: Cardiac risk, electrolyte imbalances, reduced bone density, GI and endocrine complications.
impact_on_life.emotional: Anxiety, depression, irritability; obsessive thoughts about food/weight.

comorbidities: Substance use (less common than in bulimia but possible)

psychotherapy: Family-Based Treatment (FBT/Maudsley) for adolescents with caregiver-led refeeding and graduated return of control.
Enhanced Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT-E) for adolescents/adults focusing on overvaluation of weight/shape, dietary restraint, and relapse prevention.
Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) skills for emotion regulation and distress tolerance when indicated.
Specialist supportive clinical management where CBT-E/FBT are not available.
nutrition_rehabilitation: Supervised weight restoration with individualized meal plans; regular dietitian follow-up.
Medical monitoring for refeeding syndrome: check phosphorus, potassium, magnesium; gradual caloric increases as clinically indicated.
Normalize eating patterns (3 meals + 2–3 snacks), address fear foods using graded exposure.
medical_management: Frequent vitals/weights, ECGs when bradycardic/QTc risk; monitor electrolytes and hydration.
Inpatient/residential/partial hospitalization levels of care when unstable or outpatient fails.
Calcium/vitamin D for bone health; consider physiologic estrogen replacement in adolescents with prolonged amenorrhea after nutritional rehabilitation.
medications: No medication alone treats AN; psychotherapy and nutrition are first-line.
Olanzapine (atypical antipsychotic) may aid weight gain and reduce ruminative anxiety/obsessions about weight/shape in some patients.
SSRIs (e.g., fluoxetine, sertraline) may help comorbid depression/anxiety particularly after partial weight restoration; limited benefit at very low weight.
Avoid bupropion due to seizure risk in eating disorders, especially with purging.
For osteoporosis risk: address malnutrition first; endocrinology may consider bone-protective strategies if persistent low BMD.
lifestyle_interventions: Structured routines, sleep hygiene, and stress management.
Limit compulsive exercise; reintroduce movement under medical guidance when nutritionally stable.
Family meal support; reduce scale checking and body-checking behaviors.
care_coordination: Collaborate among primary care, psychiatry, therapist, dietitian, school/coach; crisis/safety planning for suicidality or medical decompensation.

treatment_goals: Restore weight/growth trajectory and medical stability.
Normalize eating patterns and reduce dietary restraint/compensatory behaviors.
Reduce overvaluation of weight/shape and cognitive rigidity.
Prevent relapse through skills, supports, and follow-up.
missed_diagnosis_factors: Normal BMI in early stages or in atypical presentations with significant weight suppression but not underweight.
Athletes with coach-sanctioned restriction/exercise framed as ‘discipline’.
Primary care focus on GI complaints or amenorrhea without screening for eating behaviors.
Masking by wearing loose clothing; denial of illness severity.
overdiagnosis_factors: Dieting or weight loss due to medical illness misclassified without core cognitive features.
ARFID misidentified as AN when motivation is sensory/aversive rather than weight/shape concerns.
Cultural or religious fasting interpreted as psychopathology without functional impairment.
Transient adolescent dieting without fear of weight gain or body image disturbance.

type: Restricting type (no recurrent binge eating or purging in last 3 months)
Binge-eating/purging type (recurrent binge eating or purging in last 3 months)

warning_signs: Bradycardia, syncope, chest pain, shortness of breath, seizures, or confusion (medical emergency).
Rapid weight loss, refusal to eat, persistent vomiting, or electrolyte derangements.
Cold intolerance, hair loss, lanugo, amenorrhea/oligomenorrhea.
self_help_strategies: Seek support from trusted caregivers/peers; avoid pro-dieting/pro-ED media.
Schedule regular meals/snacks with support; reduce body checking and scale use.
Use coping skills for anxiety after meals (paced breathing, grounding, brief distraction).
Maintain medical and therapy appointments; share concerns early.

childhood_preteen: Early dieting disguised as ‘health choices’; growth faltering; increased rigidity around routines.
adolescence: Social withdrawal from shared meals; school/athletics impairment; amenorrhea in menstruating individuals.
adulthood: Work impairment, infertility concerns; chronic medical complications (bone, cardiac, GI) if longstanding.

first_person_statements: I genuinely believed I looked huge even when I could see my ribs. The mirror showed me something completely different from what everyone else saw.
Eating felt like failure. Every bite came with guilt and fear that I'd lose control and gain weight.
My life revolved around calories, exercise, and the scale. I lost friendships, my period stopped, and I was freezing all the time, but I couldn't stop.
Recovery was terrifying. Gaining weight felt like the worst thing in the world, but my therapist and family helped me see I was worth more than a number.
I thought restricting made me disciplined and strong, but it actually made me weak, foggy, and miserable. Getting better gave me my life back.
The eating disorder voice told me I wasn't sick enough for help. I wish I'd reached out sooner instead of waiting until I was in the hospital.

real_life_examples: A 15-year-old runner progressively restricts calories and increases training after a coach comments on her 'race weight.' Over months she loses 20 pounds, develops bradycardia (heart rate 42), and stops getting her period. Parents bring her to her pediatrician, who refers to an eating disorder program. Family-Based Treatment (FBT) empowers her parents to supervise refeeding while a medical team monitors vitals weekly. After 6 months of weight restoration, her heart rate normalizes, menses return, and she follows a safe return-to-sport plan with her dietitian and therapist.

A 19-year-old college student with a history of perfectionism begins restricting intake after gaining the 'freshman 15.' She eats only vegetables and protein, weighs all portions, and exercises 2 hours daily. She also purges after eating 'forbidden' foods like pizza or dessert. Her BMI drops to 16.5, and she becomes socially isolated. Outpatient CBT-E targets overvaluation of weight/shape and rigid food rules, while a dietitian guides structured meal plans with gradual exposure to fear foods. Low-dose olanzapine reduces intrusive thoughts about weight and food, enabling her to gain weight and reduce purging. After a year of treatment, she achieves a healthy weight and maintains recovery through college graduation.

A 13-year-old starts following 'clean eating' influencers online and begins eliminating food groups, claiming they're 'unhealthy.' Within 6 months, she's eating only plain chicken, steamed broccoli, and rice cakes, and her weight drops from the 60th to the 10th percentile. She becomes irritable, withdrawn, and obsessed with food prep. Her parents initially think she's just being health-conscious, but her pediatrician identifies faltering growth and refers for evaluation. FBT helps her parents take control of meals, and a therapist works with her on cognitive distortions. With consistent support and medical monitoring for refeeding risk, she regains weight and returns to age-appropriate flexibility with food.

A 25-year-old woman with a demanding job begins intermittent fasting, which escalates into severe calorie restriction. She skips lunch daily, eats minimal dinners, and over-exercises at the gym. Her BMI drops to 15, and she experiences dizziness, hair loss, and amenorrhea. She denies illness severity until she faints at work. Inpatient treatment stabilizes her medically, followed by a step-down to partial hospitalization where she participates in CBT-E, meal support, and group therapy. A dietitian guides weight restoration, and an SSRI helps manage comorbid anxiety. After 4 months of intensive treatment and ongoing outpatient follow-up, she achieves medical stability and begins rebuilding her career and social life.

A 16-year-old male wrestler is encouraged by his coach to 'cut weight' for a lower weight class. He begins restricting, using saunas, and spitting into cups to shed water weight. Over the season, his restriction becomes entrenched; he fears eating normally and becomes preoccupied with staying lean. His parents notice he's eating very little at home, and his school nurse finds his heart rate is 48. A sports medicine physician diagnoses anorexia nervosa and removes him from wrestling. FBT, combined with family meal support and education for the coach about safe weight management, helps him restore weight. He transitions to a different sport without weight classes and maintains recovery with periodic check-ins.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve overvaluation of weight and shape, fear of weight gain, and may include binge eating and purging behaviors.
comparisons.differences: Anorexia nervosa is characterized by significantly low body weight, while bulimia nervosa typically occurs at normal or above-normal weight. In anorexia, restriction is the primary behavior (with or without binge/purge episodes), whereas bulimia centers on recurrent binge-purge cycles.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve significant food restriction that can lead to weight loss, nutritional deficiency, and medical complications.
comparisons.differences: ARFID is driven by sensory sensitivities, fear of aversive consequences (choking, vomiting), or lack of interest in eating—not by concerns about weight or body shape. People with ARFID typically do not have distorted body image or fear of weight gain, which are hallmarks of anorexia nervosa.

comparisons.condition: Major Depressive Disorder with appetite loss
comparisons.similarities: Both can involve decreased appetite, weight loss, fatigue, and social withdrawal.
comparisons.differences: In depression, appetite loss is due to low mood and lack of pleasure in eating, without preoccupation with weight or body shape. In anorexia nervosa, restriction is intentional and driven by fear of weight gain and overvaluation of thinness. Treating the depression typically restores appetite, whereas anorexia requires specialized eating disorder treatment.

comparisons.similarities: Both involve rigid, ritualistic behaviors, high anxiety, and intrusive thoughts. People with anorexia often exhibit perfectionism and compulsive behaviors around food, exercise, and body checking.
comparisons.differences: In OCD, obsessions and compulsions are ego-dystonic (recognized as excessive and distressing), whereas in anorexia, restrictive behaviors are often ego-syntonic (aligned with goals and identity, especially early in illness). Anorexia's core focus is on weight and shape, not the broader range of obsessions seen in OCD.

faqs.question: Is anorexia nervosa just about wanting to be thin?
faqs.answer: No. While fear of weight gain and overvaluation of thinness are central, anorexia is a complex mental health condition involving biological, psychological, and environmental factors. It's not a choice or simply vanity—it's a serious illness that requires medical and psychological treatment.

faqs.question: Can males have anorexia nervosa?
faqs.answer: Yes. Although more common in females, anorexia nervosa affects people of all genders. Males may be underdiagnosed due to stigma and misconceptions that eating disorders only affect women. Symptoms and treatment are similar across genders.

faqs.question: Do you have to be extremely underweight to have anorexia?
faqs.answer: No. 'Atypical anorexia' describes individuals who meet all criteria for anorexia nervosa but are not underweight, often because they started at a higher weight. Significant weight loss from a higher baseline, combined with fear of weight gain and body image disturbance, still warrants diagnosis and treatment.

faqs.question: Will treatment make me gain too much weight?
faqs.answer: Treatment aims to restore a healthy weight range for your age, sex, and developmental trajectory—not to make you 'fat.' Weight restoration is medically supervised, gradual, and part of comprehensive care that also addresses thoughts, behaviors, and overall well-being.

faqs.question: Can anorexia nervosa be cured?
faqs.answer: Full recovery is possible. Many people achieve lasting remission with early, evidence-based treatment like Family-Based Treatment (FBT) or Enhanced Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT-E). Recovery involves not just weight restoration but also normalizing eating patterns, reducing preoccupation with weight/shape, and improving quality of life.

faqs.question: What is 'refeeding syndrome' and why is it a concern?
faqs.answer: Refeeding syndrome is a potentially life-threatening shift in electrolytes (especially phosphorus, potassium, and magnesium) that can occur when nutrition is reintroduced too quickly after starvation. Medical teams monitor labs closely and increase calories gradually to prevent this complication during weight restoration.

faqs.question: Is anorexia nervosa genetic?
faqs.answer: There is a significant genetic component—heritability is estimated around 50–60%. Having a family history of eating disorders, anxiety, or mood disorders increases risk. However, genes interact with environmental factors (e.g., diet culture, stress, trauma) to influence whether someone develops anorexia.

faqs.question: Can anorexia nervosa affect my bones and heart permanently?
faqs.answer: Prolonged malnutrition can cause lasting complications, including low bone density (osteopenia/osteoporosis) and cardiac changes. Early treatment and weight restoration improve outcomes. Bone health can improve with nutrition, weight restoration, and sometimes hormone therapy, though some deficits may persist if illness is longstanding.

faqs.question: What is Family-Based Treatment (FBT) and who is it for?
faqs.answer: FBT (also called Maudsley therapy) is an evidence-based outpatient treatment for adolescents with anorexia nervosa. Parents take an active role in supervising refeeding and weight restoration, then gradually return control to the teen as they recover. It's most effective when started early and with family involvement.

faqs.question: What's the difference between restricting type and binge-eating/purging type?
faqs.answer: Restricting type involves only food restriction and possibly excessive exercise, with no regular binge eating or purging. Binge-eating/purging type includes episodes of binge eating and/or purging (vomiting, laxatives, diuretics) in addition to restriction. Both types require significantly low weight for an anorexia diagnosis.

faqs.question: Why can't I just 'eat normally' if I know restricting is harmful?
faqs.answer: Anorexia nervosa hijacks brain circuits involved in fear, reward, and self-perception. Starvation also changes brain chemistry and reinforces restriction. Eating feels threatening, not logical. Recovery requires structured support—therapy, medical monitoring, nutrition counseling, and often family or peer support—to retrain your brain and body.

faqs.question: Will I have to stop exercising completely?
faqs.answer: Initially, if you're medically unstable, exercise may be restricted to allow weight restoration and prevent cardiac risk. As you recover, movement is gradually reintroduced under medical supervision, focusing on health and enjoyment rather than calorie burning. The goal is a balanced relationship with physical activity.

faqs.question: Can I recover if I've had anorexia for many years?
faqs.answer: Yes, though recovery may take longer and involve more intensive treatment (e.g., residential or partial hospitalization). Chronic illness increases risk of medical complications and entrenched patterns, but many people with longstanding anorexia do achieve meaningful recovery with persistent, multidisciplinary care.

faqs.question: What should I do if I think my friend or family member has anorexia?
faqs.answer: Express concern calmly and without judgment. Share specific observations (e.g., 'I've noticed you're skipping meals and seem really tired'). Encourage them to talk to a trusted adult or healthcare provider. Avoid commenting on appearance or weight. Offer support, but recognize that professional help is essential.

faqs.question: Are medications effective for anorexia nervosa?
faqs.answer: No medication alone treats anorexia nervosa. Therapy (especially FBT or CBT-E) and nutritional rehabilitation are first-line. Medications like olanzapine may help with weight gain and reducing obsessive thoughts, and SSRIs can address comorbid anxiety or depression, particularly after partial weight restoration. Treatment is always multidisciplinary.

faqs.question: Why does anorexia cause hair loss and growth of fine body hair (lanugo)?
faqs.answer: Malnutrition disrupts hair growth cycles, causing hair on the scalp to thin and fall out. Lanugo—soft, downy body hair—grows as the body's attempt to conserve heat when body fat and metabolism are very low. Both typically reverse with nutritional rehabilitation and weight restoration.

faqs.question: Can you have anorexia and not realize you're underweight?
faqs.answer: Yes. Distorted body image is a core feature of anorexia nervosa. Many people genuinely perceive themselves as larger than they are, or they may intellectually recognize low weight but lack emotional insight into its seriousness. This is why external support and structured treatment are crucial.

faqs.question: Is it possible to prevent anorexia nervosa?
faqs.answer: While there's no guaranteed prevention, reducing risk factors helps: promote balanced attitudes toward food and body image, avoid weight-related teasing, address perfectionistic traits with healthy coping skills, and foster open communication. Early intervention at the first signs of disordered eating significantly improves outcomes.

content.when_to_seek_help: Immediate medical evaluation for fainting, chest pain, heart rate <50 (adolescents) or <40 (adults), rapid weight loss, persistent vomiting, or electrolyte symptoms. Seek specialized eating-disorder care if restriction, fear of weight gain, or body-image distress interfere with health or functioning.

positive_factors: Rapid weight restoration and medical stabilization
Lower illness chronicity; good therapeutic alliance

tiles.title: What is Anorexia Nervosa?
tiles.summary: Serious eating disorder involving severe restriction, fear of weight gain, and distorted body image.

tiles.title: Signs & Symptoms
tiles.summary: Extreme weight loss, obsessive calorie counting, excessive exercise, distorted body image, and medical complications.

tiles.title: Causes & Risk Factors
tiles.summary: Genetic vulnerability, perfectionism, anxiety traits, diet culture, weight-focused activities, and life stress.

tiles.title: How It's Diagnosed
tiles.summary: Clinical interview, medical exam, lab work, assessment of eating behaviors, weight history, and psychological symptoms.

tiles.title: Treatment Options
tiles.summary: Family-Based Treatment (FBT), CBT-E, nutritional rehabilitation, medical monitoring, and sometimes medications.

tiles.title: Medical Complications
tiles.summary: Cardiac issues, bone loss, hormone disruption, electrolyte imbalances, and increased mortality risk.

tiles.title: Recovery & Prognosis
tiles.summary: Full recovery is possible with early treatment. Family involvement and rapid weight restoration improve outcomes.

tiles.title: Living with Anorexia
tiles.summary: Structured meals, reducing body checking, managing anxiety, family support, and maintaining treatment engagement.

tiles.title: Getting Help
tiles.summary: Seek specialized eating disorder care for restriction, fear of weight gain, or medical instability.
